summary: Brick conical light of 1858 at the Delaware-Maryland line: lit 1859, dark 1978, relit by volunteers in 1982. The State of Delaware owns it.

access.note: The base is open seasonally on the Friends' schedule. The tower is closed to climbing. The State of Delaware owns the tower.

facts.agency: State of Delaware (owner); New Friends of the Fenwick Island Lighthouse (volunteer group)

events.note: Congress authorized the lighthouse on 18 August 1856, not to exceed $25,000
Tower and station buildings completed (Notice to Mariners, 29 December 1858, as LighthouseFriends reports)
First lit 1 August 1859
Third-order Fresnel lens by L. Sautter & Cie, of French manufacture
Second, larger keepers' dwelling (the nomination gives 1882; LighthouseFriends gives formal acceptance on 12 November 1881)
Wooden pile bridge to the mainland built, about 225 feet long
Fourth-order oil lamps replaced by fourth-order electric lamps (nomination)
Christmas Day 1931: keepers picked up a man from a stranded small boat, half a mile south of the light
Light electrified; the assistant keeper's post abolished (LighthouseFriends)
Coast Guard sold three-quarters of the station land, including the old dwelling, to the retired head keeper, for $1,610.79
Lighthouse automated; much of the ten-acre property sold (nomination)
Turned off by the Coast Guard on 13 December 1978
Lens and electrical lighting mechanism removed 13 December 1978; pedestal and shaft left in place
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979
Coast Guard transferred the tower to the State of Delaware on 21 September 1981; the state leased it to the Friends
Relit in 1982 as an unofficial private aid to navigation, with a less powerful light source and the returned Fresnel lens
Restoration of the tower with $400,000 from the state; rededicated July 1998
New Friends of the Fenwick Island Lighthouse formed under Winnie Lewis
State acquired the keeper's dwelling west of the lighthouse (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper's house restored as a publicly accessible space with a gift shop (State of Delaware)

corrections.why: No source read gives the current characteristic. The historic characteristic was a fixed white light with a flash of about 20 seconds every two minutes (nomination), and the Delaware office says the light was re-lit in 1982 as an unofficial private aid.
The light was first lit on 1 August 1859; 1858 was the year of completion, with exhibition delayed to 1859.
The record does not show the 1982 relighting by the State of Delaware and the Friends.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record says sources differ on whether the light is still lit. The Delaware history office says it was re-lit in 1982 as an unofficial private aid to navigation. The sources read do not give its current characteristic or whether it shows every night.
The nomination gives $23,748; LighthouseFriends gives $23,749. Both are shown as sourced; the difference is trivial.
The nomination dates it to 1882; LighthouseFriends says bids were opened in June 1881 and the house was ready for acceptance on 12 November 1881. The story gives both.
The nomination gives 2,800 gallons; LighthouseFriends gives 2,500. The story reports both.
LighthouseFriends says the light was electrified in 1936 and the assistant's post abolished; the nomination gives 1940 for automation. Both are reported.
The nomination says electric lamps replaced the oil lamps in 1899. The Board's 1900 report describes a new fourth-order lamp on 13 July, with OCR reading the year as 1890. Not resolved.
LighthouseFriends puts the shoal eight miles from the light; the Delaware history office says six miles. Both are reported.

The Lighthouse Service Bulletin and the Washington Daily News describe a voyage from Greenland to the Panama Canal with a stop in Massachusetts; LighthouseFriends describes a solo voyage to Alaska and an unconscious man. The story follows the bulletin and the newspaper.

The New Friends' list differs from the USLHS roster on several dates and spellings: Stites (1914-1927 vs 1914-1926), Gray (1927 vs 1926), Pardee (William D. vs Willis B.), Bennett (John D. vs Jehu D.), Neal/Neil Gray, Vaughn/Vaughan, Gunn/Gumm. The roster is followed for the stints; the Friends' variants are in notes.
LighthouseFriends names Paul Pepper's grandfather as an assistant keeper; the roster has no Edward G. Pepper, and William E. Pepper (1869-1885) is not linked by name alone. Not linked.

notes_for_editor: Rich station; the chapter on keepers relies on the USLHS roster (NARA registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory) and on the New Friends' keeper list, which gives different dates for several stints and some names the roster lacks (B. W. Hitchens, Levin Day). Those Friends-only names are on the roster lines with cites but no person id. The 1931 rescue depends on the 1932 Lighthouse Service Bulletin and a 1932 newspaper column; LighthouseFriends' version (solo voyage to Alaska, unconscious man) is not used. The 1855 report is read only as the nomination quotes it; the Board report is not in the local corpus (its series starts in 1891). The 1900 Board report's lamp entry is OCR-read as 1890; the nomination says 1899; not resolved. The record's characteristic 'Iso W 8s' is not supported by the sources read; the historic characteristic is in the nomination. The Fenwick Island Shoal lightship (1888-1933) is a separate record and is only mentioned here. Coordinates in the record (38.45137, -75.05495) match LighthouseFriends and ARLHS and were kept. The tower height in the record (26.0 m) and the nomination's 84 ft 5 in (25.7 m) differ by 0.3 m and were not corrected. The Friends' visiting page is titled 'summer-2018' but its content is the 2026 schedule; check it before a visit. Verification pass 2026-10-22: the NRHP text gives 1881 for the second keepers' house in section 8 ('A second lighthouse keeper's house was erected in 1881') and 1882 in section 7; the story gives the section 7 date and LighthouseFriends' 1881 bids and acceptance. The Friends' keeper list also names 'William D. Pardee' (keeper, 7/23/1910 to December 1912) and 'W. B. Paradee' (assistant, 9/9/1909 to 7/9/1910). Neither is added as a roster line because the sources do not connect them with the roster's Willis B. Pardee, who is on the roster for both posts; a human should decide whether they are one man. The story's 1931 rescue follows the bulletin (p. 12) and the Washington Daily News column of 16 January 1932 (read through newspapers.py): the column says the sailboat was 'pushed off into deep water', the bulletin says 'gotten off into deep water'; the story uses the bulletin's wording. The Board's 1900 report entry reads 'July 13, 1890' in the OCR text; the nomination's 1899 is given as the alternative date and the year is not resolved. The Friends' visiting page is titled 'summer-2018' but shows the 2026 schedule.
